extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, designers and artists concerned with architectural colour and ornamentation
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for applying colour and ornament to architecture: how colour relates to form, where and how to use natural materials versus paint, the hierarchy of sculptural and coloured elements, mediums appropriate to architectural decoration, and the signs of vitality in architectural imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer noble material over mechanical paint
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nobler natural materials (e.g., variegated stone) rather than painted colour laid on by common workmen; mechanized or vulgar colouring is more offensive than imperfection in carving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If clients demand painted colour that would be applied coarsely, it is better to alter design to employ naturally coloured stone even at the cost of some intricacy. The 'lovely and mellow hues of the natural stone' should be preferred to painted colour applied by a mechanical hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of colour from form
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural colour should be 'visibly independent of form' — arranged on a system separate from the architectural shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make colour 'follow' the architectural forms (e.g., avoid applying vertical colour lines to a vertically fluted column). Treat colour as a distinct layer, like the colouring of a shell, flower, or animal rather than the colouring of a landscape group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never paint a column with vertical lines; cross it
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid painting columns with vertical colour lines that simply mimic the form; instead apply cross-patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rule from the text: 'Never paint a column with vertical lines, but always cross it.' This prevents colour from merely accentuating form in a literal, mechanical way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give separate mouldings separate colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid assigning a distinct colour to each moulding or sculptural element as if colouring independent pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than painting leaves/figures one colour and their ground another, 'vary both the ground and the figures with the same harmony.' Colour should form a unified system, not a set of isolated painted bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place variegation on broad surfaces; avoid colour on points of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The best location for variegated colour is flat walls and broad shafts; be shy of putting it on capitals, mouldings, or points of formal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: animals are mottled on breast and back, rarely on paws or around eyes. Similarly, put variegation boldly on broad surfaces, simplify colour when form is rich, and simplify form where colour is rich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify colour when form is rich, and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an inverse balance between the complexity of form and the complexity of colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If architectural form is elaborate, simplify the colour scheme; if form is simple, you may allow more complex colour patterning. This preserves clarity and avoids visual conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carve delicate ornaments in white marble and leave them
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals and graceful sculptural ornaments are best executed in pure white marble and left uncoloured (or very cautiously touched).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White marble best displays fine sculptural completion. Colouring such elements risks deadening their carved grace; touch only points and borders, and do so in a system non-concurrent with their forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour boundaries should be simple or soft, not highly refined
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural colour patterns often have soft, irregular, or 'rude' outlines; architectural colour should emulate that simplicity rather than refined, precise outlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour is 'best seen' in simple or rude forms; do not attempt to 'refine' colour arrangements to the precision of drawn forms — e.g., you cannot produce a good painted window with highly finished figure-drawing and perfect colour simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect colour and perfect form cannot be united
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of simultaneously having perfect line/form and perfect colour is unattainable; improving one tends to diminish the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the author puts it: 'You will lose perfection of colour as you give perfection of line.' Design choices must prioritize which quality is dominant in a given element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple mass-colour elements: zones, cloudings, flamings, spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural colour patterns should be composed from simple elemental types observed in nature: zones (bands), cloudings, flame-like streaks, and spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements may vary in sharpness and complexity (zones into fines, flaming into triangles or stars, spots into stains or geometric shapes). Their arrangement and relative quantities determine harmonious colour effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape of colour elements must serve quantity and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness of colour shapes depends on how they determine relative quantities and regulate interactions between colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce points or edges of one colour between breadths of others; triangular and barred forms are convenient. Curved/refined outlines tend to deaden colour and confuse the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved/refined outlines deaden colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Refined curved outlines reduce the vibrancy and legibility of colour patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer angular, even 'quaint' or 'angular' dispositions for architectural colouring; curved, luxurious outlines that are beneficial to superb drawing will often weaken architectural colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quaint or angular patterns can be effective in colour even if poor in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns and heraldic or reticulated features that are monstrosities in sculptural form may be delightful as colour themes if lines are not fluttering or over-twisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Styles (e.g., Tudor reticulation) that sacrifice spaciousness and breadth can still yield 'highly beautiful' coloured surfaces when treated as pattern rather than sculptural form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monochrome design as an intermediate between colouring and carving
rubrics_metrics.description: Monochrome (single-colour figure on contrasting ground) is a mode between painting and sculpture, admitting simplicity of contour and for the first time allowing colour to be concurrent with outlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monochrome figures are most abstract and demand excessive simplicity of form to work architecturally; they are progressive/imperfect compared with high sculpture and are best used in specific contexts (e.g., St. Michele of Lucca examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of architectural decoration (four kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Pure architectural decoration is limited to four kinds, ranging from sculpture-dominant to wholly abstract colour patterning:
1) Organic form dominant
2) Organic form sub-dominant
3) Organic form abstracted to outline (monochrome)
4) Organic forms entirely lost (geometrical patterns/cloudings)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage admits progressively more concurrent use of colour with outlines and more abstraction; they 'glide almost imperceptibly' into each other and should be chosen according to the intended relation between sculptural form and colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic form dominant — sculptural primacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where organic form is dominant: true independent sculpture and alto-relievo; rich capitals and mouldings; complete in form and to be left in pure white marble or only very cautiously coloured in points and borders, in a system non-concurrent with their forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour must be subordinate to sculptural completion; colour touches only sparingly and not in a way that follows the sculpture's outlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic form sub-dominant — reduced depth and bolder colour
rubrics_metrics.description: When organic form is sub-dominant: basso-relievo or intaglio with more abstract contours; colour may be applied more boldly in exact proportion to the reduced depth and fullness, yet still non-concurrent with contours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As depth and sculptural fullness reduce, increased colour may be acceptable, but preserve a non-concurrent system between colour and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic form abstracted to outline — monochrome concurrent with outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: At the stage where organic forms are reduced to outline (monochrome design), colour may become concurrent with outlines — i.e., the figure can be detached in one colour from a ground of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This admits a different relationship between colour and form but requires simplicity of contour and abstraction to function architecturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic forms entirely lost — geometric/abstract colour patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: When organic forms are entirely subordinated, decoration becomes geometric patterns or variable cloudings using the wildest colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most abstract end of the spectrum and appropriate for surfaces where sculptural form is absent or deliberately suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose medium according to abstraction and architectural role
rubrics_metrics.description: Different pictorial media vary in architectural applicability: mosaic (highly abstract, brilliant colour masses) and decorative fresco fit architecture best; pictorial fresco becomes principal and may cease to be the architect's concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mosaic and decorative fresco are most suitable for architectural ornamentation because of their abstraction; high pictorial work (e.g., Sistine-style) often should be left to painters and treated after building completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour patterns should be naturally irregular and allow looseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural colour boundaries are often irregular, blotched, and imperfect; architecture should accept a degree of looseness, variation, and even harshness in colour which would be monstrous in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to render colour with draughtsmanship-level precision is likely to fail; artists should study natural variegated forms and emulate their softer, more accidental boundaries for effective colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture must express the life of the maker — avoid deadness
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignity and pleasure of architecture depend on the visible expression of intellectual life that produced it; architecture that lacks this is 'dead' and oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware formal practice without vitality: mere copying or superficial revival, executed 'without paying interest' or 'without choice', leads to dead architecture. Aim for works showing evident energy and assimilation of influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthy imitation must pay interest: frankness and audacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation in architecture is acceptable and even noble when it is energetic, frank, and audacious — openly borrowing but reworking and subordinating fragments into a new, harmonious whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vital imitation shows 'frankness' — no effort to conceal sources — and 'audacity' in re-arrangement. Borrowed elements should be integrated and transformed to fit the architect's own instincts rather than copied servilely.
